caseno: Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal Nos. 106 and 107 of 1993.
lawyer:
Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md. Sajjadul Huq, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Petitioner. (In both the cases).
No one ----- For the Respondent.
parties:
Al-Hajj Mirjahan ----- Petitioner. [In CP No. 106 of 1993]
Vs.
AI-Hajj Md. Rafique Miah ----- Petitioner. [In CP No. 107 of 1993]
Vs.
Golden Biscuit Co ----- Respondent. [In both cases.]
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed CJ : Two co-sharer landlords have filed these two leave petitions separately and the tenant is the common Respondent in both the petitions. The High Court Division, by two separate judgments, bearing the same date, 6 January 1993, allowed two corresponding Civil Revision Nos. 674 and 675 of 1990 and directed thereby the Rent Controller to accept a monthly deposit of rent made by the tenant under section 19 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance. 

 2. Respondent-tenant, M/s Golden Biscuit Company was monthly tenant in respect of the premises in question, carrying on business there and paying rent regularly to its owner Alhaj Md. Ashraf Ali for last 22 years. This landlord, by two registered deeds dated 2 November, 1987, sold away the premises to the Petitioners, Alhaj Mirjahan and Alhaj Md. Rafiqure Miah in equal share, and by a letter dated 16 November 1987, advised the tenant to pay rent henceforward to the two new landlords. The two purchasers-landlords, also informed the tenant in a similar manner about the change of ownership of the premises. The rent for the premises was Taka 1200.00 per month. The tenant remitted the rent for the month of November 1987 by postal money order to the new landlords. Allegation of the tenant is, that the new landlords purposely avoided receipt of the money order by constantly remaining absent from their houses. Thereupon, the tenant filed an application before the Rent Controller within the prescribed time to deposit the rent. But upon an objection from the two landlords, the deposit was refused. The tenant filed an appeal, but it was also dismissed by the Subordinate judge. Thereupon, the tenant came to the High Court Division with two revisional applications, as mentioned above, and obtained a favourable order in each case. 

 3. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, learned Advocate, has appeared for the petitioner in both the matters. He contends that the tenant was not entitled to make the deposit at the first instance as he did not pay or tender the rent personally to the landlords. The learned Advocate has referred to section 19(1) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance and has submitted that if a tenant offers the rent, and the landlord refuses to accept it, then the tenant will remit the rent by postal money order and that if the postal money order is returned undelivered, then only the tenant will make the deposit with the Rent Controller. In this case, the learned Advocate contends, remittance of the rent by Money Order without first approaching the Landlord with "personal tender" is not contemplated in law. The learned Advocate, however, does not dispute that rent for the month of November 1987, that is, the month in which the premises was sold, was remitted by postal money order well within the prescribed time. The dispute is as to the manner of tendering the rent. The learned Advocate has failed to show us any law which requires that rent is to be paid or tendered personally by the tenant to the landlord. If, for instance, the landlord resides in a different place, the tenant may send the rent by Money Order or by Bank Cheque or Bank Draft according to any arrangement between the landlord and the tenant. In the instant case, the tenant remitted the rent well within the prescribed time and when the money order was returned undelivered, the tenant was entitled to make the deposit. 

 4. Before the Rent Controller, the landlords, however, took a different ground of objection, which was that, by remitting half of the rent to one landlord and another half to other landlord the tenant bifurcated the tenancy itself. The ground was totally baseless, for, when the premises was sold to two different persons under two separate registered deeds, the payment of the rent to both the landlords who became co-sharers in the premises did not violate any provision of law. It is for the new landlords to give instruction to the tenant to whom the rent was to be paid. Section 19(2) of the Ordinance permits the tenant to deposit rent in case of any bonafide doubt or dispute as to the person entitled to receive the rent. We do not find any wrong in the impugned order of the High Court Division allowing the tenant's application for making deposit of rent.
